Andrew Bielecki VASSALBORO LD 1456
Dear Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and Members of the Committee,
My name is Andrew Bielecki, and I am a resident of Vassalboro. I also serve as the Director of Operations for Sidereal Farm Brewery in Vassalboro. Thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony in support of the proposed changes to this bill.
Our small brewery began operations in 2022 on our 22-acre farm. Starting with five employees who resided in Vassalboro, Winslow, and Bangor, we have since grown to create 15 jobs, now employing residents from Vassalboro and many surrounding communities. This growth has been made possible by the significant support from Maine's legislation and the craft beer community. Alongside the increase in our workforce, we have also made substantial capital improvements, including the addition of numerous fermentation vessels and a large beer garden over the past two and a half years.
As the current law is structured, the allowance of virtually unlimited retail licenses without any significant production requirements or investment in our Maine economy is concerning. This situation has the potential to devalue the investments we have made in our employees, land, and equipment. Clarifying the language in this statute will help ensure a fair and equal access to the market for businesses like ours, which in turn will secure the continued investment in Maine-based job creation and the local manufacturing of craft beverages.
Once again, I appreciate your time and consideration today. I respectfully ask for your support of this important legislation.
Sincerely, Andrew

Thank you Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Committee:
My name is Dan Kleban, I am a resident of Cumberland and I'm the Co-Founder and Co-Owner of Maine Beer Company. I appreciate the opportunity to weigh in on the proposed changes and add my voice in support of this bill.
My brother and I started Maine Beer Company in 2009 with the goal of creating a company purposed with doing good through great beer. "Do what's right", our motto, is at the forefront of every decision we make, from how we treat our employees, to the beer we brew, to taking care of the world around us.
When we started our business, there weren't very many breweries in the state, and the common assumption was a 1:1 ratio of brewery license to retail license. At the time, we couldn't even charge customers for samples of our beer, and tasting rooms were virtually non-existent. The evolution of the industry allowed us to grow our business, expanding on our Freeport location and investing millions of dollars in equipment and infrastructure. This growth required more staff, and we now employ over 100 employees, providing 100% company-paid health insurance and 5% or more towards retirement.
We are proud to have donated almost $4,000,000 to nonprofits since 2009, and much of our support stays in Maine, helping small communities and preserving the environment.
While it is great to see innovation of business models within the craft beer industry, the the current law allows for a virtually unlimited number of retail licenses and lacks the requirement of meaningful production requirements in order to open and operate.
I'm concerned that the lack of a clear definition around "manufacturing facility" poses a risk to the craft breweries who could be denied access to market by businesses posing as craft breweries but not satisfying the technical requirements of actually brewing beer. By adapting the statute, we will better ensure a fair and supportive playing field long term for Maine based job creation, small business manufacturing, and the continued health of locally made craft beverages.
Thank you for your time and consideration today, and I ask for you to support this important legislation.

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs: I am Louis Luchini and I'm the Director of the Bureau of Alcoholic Beverages and
Lottery Operations. I'm here to testify in support of LD 1456, An Act to Expand the Number of Onpremises Retail Liquor Licenses a Liquor Manufacturer May Be Issued.
Under current law, a small in-state manufacturer is eligible for one license for on-premises consumption (often called a chapter 43 license) per manufacturing facility, provided both establishments have the same maj ority ownership. This applies to small breweries, small wineries, and small distilleries that are
licensed under 28-A MRS �l355-A. This is a general exception to the three-tier system which prohibits
cross-tier ownership.
This bill proposes to increase the allowable number of chapter 43 on-premises licenses to three per manufacturing facility. The bill also places a cap on the total number of on-premises licenses owned by
a person to six.
The Bureau supports LD 1456, and views this as an economic development measure that will expand business opportunities for Maine-based entrepreneurs. We appreciate the work of President Daughtry
and the Maine Brewers Guild in developing this legislation. Maine's craft breweries, in conjunction with the Maine Brewers Guild, have done tremendous work over the past decade to make Maine a destination for craft beer. The industry's economic impact to Maine's economy is significant, as outlined in a 2022 report by the University of Maine entitled, "The Economic Contribution of the Craft Brewing Industry in Maine" . * This bill will also support those small distilleries, wineries, cideries and meaderies that offer tremendous Maine products.
Increasing the allowance to three retail locations per manufacturing facility will provide growth
opportunities for industry participants. We are in support.
Thank you for your consideration. I'm happy to answer questions.

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Veterans and Legal Affairs, my name is Mattie Daughtry. I serve as President of the Maine Senate
and proudly represent Senate District 23, including Brunswick, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal,
Chebeague Island, and part of Yarmouth. In my life outside this building, I am the founder, owner, and operator of Moderation Brewing, located in my hometown of Brunswick.
On behalf of the Maine Brewers Guild, I am proud to present to you LD 1456 "An Act to Expand the Number of On-Premise Retail Liquor Licenses A Liquor Manufacturer May Be Issued."

I want to start by noting that this bill does not "expand" the number of on-premise retail liquor licenses - commonly known as "Chapter 43 s" or "brewpubs" - but rather restricts those licenses
total of six. Current law allows for a virtually unlimited number of retail licenses, which when

to a

combined with minimal production requirements, has created an environment where individuals and
'
entities can call themselves a "brewery" and then use the current law to open a brewpub without

really manufacturing local craft beer. That is because production requirements in our current law are
minimal -- allowing for a brewery to ferment beer in a bucket - in order to obtain the manufacturers

privilege of selling directly to consumers for on-premise consumption.

This lack of production minimums has been a source of disagreement and discussion within the brewery industry for many years. Recently, however, Maine craft breweries have noted more and more establishments holding themselves out as "Maine Craft Breweries" while producing minimal
actual product for public consumption and taking full advantage of the ability to open an often lucrative "brewpub."

This proposed bill would help protect true manufacturers of craft beer by limiting access to Chapter 43 licenses to a total of six and imposing liquor production minimums for access to licenses four, five, and six. This change, while technically rolling back access to brewpub licenses, will help ensure that those accessing these licenses are truly committed to the production of craft beer. It will help
support brewers who are investing in equipment, high quality ingredients, and the Maine brand by
allowing them additional access to brewpub licenses if they meet meaningful production minimums.

Chapter 43 licenses were originally designed to help support breweries and other liquor
manufacturers who wished to introduce their product to consumers and to give them an opportunity to interact with and learn about the manufacturing process. They were never intended to become a work around for those really looking to operate a bar and/or restaurant while not producing any actual
liquor.

Thank you Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Committee:
My name is Michael Fava, I am a resident of South Portland and I'm here today as the Co-Founder of Sacred Profane Brewery. I appreciate the opportunity to weigh in on the proposed changes and add my voice in support of this bill.
As a Maine craft brewer, I see that the current law allows for a virtually unlimited amount of retail licenses and that the absence of meaningful production requirements devalue the investment I've made in my brewery and employees. 10045570:
Testimony in Support of LD1456 Nicholas Bonadies, President, Belleflower Brewing Company
Thank you, Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and Members of the Committee:
My name is Nicholas Bonadies, and I am a resident of Portland, here today as the President of Belleflower Brewing Company. I appreciate the opportunity to speak with you and to offer my strong support for the proposed legislation.
Belleflower is a family-owned and operated brewery, run by my family and the Page family. We currently employ 15 people, including the owners. Like many others in Maine's brewing community, we are proud to be part of a vibrant and growing industry that is deeply rooted in our local economy. Maine's unique natural resources--like the bounty of Androscoggin County and the waters of Lake Sebago--have helped make our state a national leader in craft brewing.
Since launching our relatively small brewery, we've invested over a million dollars into equipment, professional services, and skilled trades. The cost and complexity of building a true production-capable facility is significant--and its impact is far-reaching, from the construction work itself to the malt we purchase from Maine farmers.
But the reality is: we operate on a very narrow seasonal window. Summer tourism keeps many of us afloat, as visitors seek to experience the flavors, stories, and craftsmanship that make Maine special. They come to connect with a piece of what it means to be a Mainer--something we strive to represent through our brands.
Unfortunately, under current law, retail licenses can be obtained with few constraints--no meaningful requirements for production capacity or space. This undermines the value of the hard work and investment that go into building a true production brewery. It can also confuse consumers about what a brewery is and does. As the industry matures, we're seeing more businesses doing the bare minimum to qualify for licensing, without contributing meaningfully to the state's manufacturing economy.
We believe Maine breweries can do more--should do more--to honor the legacy built by the brewers who came before us. Updating the statute to ensure fair, equitable access to market for all beverage manufacturers will help maintain a healthy, competitive landscape. It will support job creation, reward real investment in manufacturing, and protect the integrity of Maine's craft beverage industry.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I urge you to support this important legislation. I'm happy to answer any questions or continue this discussion further.

Maine Brewers' Guild PO Box 2817 South Portland, ME 04116 4/23/25
Good afternoon Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and distinguished members of the Veterans & Legal Affairs Committee:
My name is Sarah Bryan, I am a resident of Portland and I'm here today as the Executive Director of The Maine Brewers Guild members, who have voted to stand united in support of the proposed changes of LD1456.
The Maine Brewers Guild is a nonprofit dedicated to promoting and protecting the craft beer industry in Maine for the past 30 years. Even before our inception, since the mid 1980's, Maine has been at the forefront of the craft beer movement. Our state is home to over 150 breweries; we directly employ thousands of residents, contribute nearly $700M dollars in economic impact per annum, conservatively utilize more than 4M pounds of Maine-grown ingredients in the brewing process every year, and are distinguished as the second highest number of breweries per capita in the country.
We are united in the perspective that the existing law and the lack of meaningful production requirements, does not recognize, incentivize or adequately protect Maine brewery investment or local brewery employment. Instead it is being utilized to obtain unlimited amounts of Chapter 43 licenses, without a requisite to manufacture anything beyond minimal amounts of alcoholic beverage products. We believe that this activity runs afoul of the intent of the law and results in working breweries losing representation and market access.
By adapting the statute to ensure equal access-to-market for all beverage manufacturers, we will better ensure a fair and supportive playing field long term for Maine based job creation, small business manufacturing, and the continued health of locally made craft beverages. Our due diligence has turned up no records of existing breweries that currently extend outside the proposed location cap of 6, and have worked consistently with our colleagues in both wine and distilled spirits who are supportive of these changes.
Maine-brewed beer is, in many ways, an essential bellwether industry for both Maine manufacturing and Maine tourism sectors. The work is difficult and expensive, but thrives upon the foundation that quality goods made by hardworking people in the small towns and cities of Maine, will always make a positive impact in local agriculture, the community and the Maine economy. It is for these reasons I urge you to support the proposed changes to this bill.
Sincerely,
Sarah Bryan Executive Director, Maine Brewers' Guild
10046066:
Thank you Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Committee:
My name is Will Fisher and I'm a resident of Portland. I'm here today as a Founder of Austin Street Brewery. I appreciate the opportunity to weigh in on the proposed changes and add my voice in support of LD 1456.
Austin Street Brewery was founded in 2014 and we're honored to be celebrating our 11th anniversary on May 17th; if you're in the area, please join us at 115 Fox Street in Portland (shameless plug). We started Austin Street with our own money and have grown the business organically over the last decade. In fact, my co-founder, Jake and I, still own 100% of Austin Street. With great pride and dedication to Maine craft beer, we have grown the brewery to support 16 employees and have produced over 600,000 gallons of beer, which has been distributed all over Maine and New England.
Craft beer is not a get rich quick endeavor; in fact, it's not a get rich ever! We do this because we love going to work and we get a chance to create something that promotes community and builds meaningful relationships. Unfortunately, it's not all cold beer and good times. Costs have been accelerating since 2020 and most of our bottom line has been eroded. For example, in 2014 we charged $105 for a keg of beer and 11 years later, we charge $110 for that same keg (a 5% increase). All the while our cost of goods have gone up almost 40%. As a specialty product, we don't have the liberty to raise prices 40% like other markets; customers are already paying a premium to enjoy Austin Street instead of a national brand.
Maine craft beer is recognized around the country and the world. This creates incredible value and we rely on that reputation to keep the doors open. Our staff is made up of 100% Mainers, our industry requires us to work in-person, and all of our beer is brewed in-house. In a world of work-from-home and fractional services, traditional beer production has become a bit of an anomaly. There's no wrong way to brew a great beer, but it's important that Maine breweries are able to protect their craft and the "Maine brand" with a certain level of sanctity.
I've been a part of the Maine Brewers' Guild legislative committee for as long as I can remember and have been a part of several significant legislative changes. With my firsthand experience, I can assure you Austin Street would not be making beer today if it wasn't for these changes. LD 1456 does a great job of defining and protecting what makes Maine beer so special while allowing ALL Maine-based beverage producers the ability to flourish. These changes are simply the next step in a series of healthy updates. Our fearless Executive Director, Sarah Bryan, put it best:
"We're starting to see a proliferation of businesses representing themselves as craft brewers, but who technically only brew a tiny amount of beer just to satisfy the technical

requirements of their manufacturing license. By adapting the statute to ensure equal access-to-market for all beverage manufacturers, we will better ensure a fair and supportive playing field long term for Maine based job creation, small business manufacturing, and the continued health of locally made craft beverages."
Thank you for your time and consideration today, and I ask for you to support LD 1456.
I'm happy to answer questions or speak further on the subject as needed.
